bites.title: Cost multiplies: every agent adds tokens and calls
bites.body:
A single-agent call sends one system prompt, the user input and its tool definitions.

Now split that same job across a four-agent team with a supervisor. The supervisor reads the input and writes a brief. Worker 1 reads its system prompt and the brief, calls tools and writes a report. The supervisor reads the report and briefs Worker 2. Worker 2 runs its turns. The supervisor reads both reports and calls the Reviewer. One user question has quietly turned into twelve LLM calls and tens of thousands of repeated context tokens.

It is calling a meeting with six people for a decision one person could have made at their desk in five minutes.

Always calculate the token multiplier per user request before proposing a multi-agent design.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why does a multi-agent team often cost several times more tokens than a single agent for the same request?

choices.text: Providers charge a special penalty fee whenever two agents have different names
Multi-agent systems are required to use the most expensive model for every step
Every delegation, handoff and review repeats system prompts and context across multiple separate LLM calls
Single agents do not pay for input tokens

questions.explanation: Each agent turn and coordinator handoff resends prompts and context, multiplying both call count and token spend.

bites.title: Errors compound: one bad handoff spoils everything after it
bites.body:
In a chain of agents, each agent trusts the structured output or summary handed to it by the previous agent.

If Agent 1 misreads a date as 2024 instead of 2025, or drops a crucial constraint when summarising the user's request, Agent 2 and Agent 3 never see the original source to notice the slip. They build elaborate, polished analysis on top of a false premise.

It is the party game Whisper Down the Lane: a tiny slip between the first two players turns the message into nonsense by the end of the line.

Validate key facts and pass references to original source IDs across handoffs so later agents or gates can verify critical figures.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: How can a small mistake in the first agent spoil the work of an entire multi-agent team?

choices.text: Later agents always delete the first agent's output
Errors automatically cancel each other out across three agents
Downstream agents work from the first agent's summary or handoff without seeing the original input, so they build on the mistake
Only the last agent in a chain can make mistakes

questions.explanation: Information loss or distortion at a handoff propagates forward unless key facts are checked against original sources.

bites.title: Agents that loop, stall, or argue
bites.body:
Put two or more autonomous agents in a conversation without tight rules and they can fail in uniquely comical ways.

Two agents can fall into a **politeness loop** ("Thank you!" / "You're welcome, let me know if you need anything else!" / "Thanks again!"). A generator and an overly strict critic can **argue** for ten rounds as fixing one rule breaks another. Or a supervisor can **stall**, repeatedly calling the same search worker that keeps returning "no results found".

It is two people holding a door for each other in a corridor, both saying "After you" while nobody walks through.

Prevent these with structured outputs instead of chatty prose, state progress checks and hard turn limits.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What is a common cause of two agents getting stuck in a loop?

choices.text: Setting a strict maximum step count on the workflow
Using structured JSON fields to signal completion
Unstructured chat handoffs or conflicting critic rules with no progress check or turn cap
Running deterministic code between steps

questions.explanation: Replacing free-form chat between agents with structured state updates and hard iteration limits stops polite or argumentative loops.

bites.title: Tracing a failure back to the agent that caused it
bites.body:
When a user reports that the final report contained a wrong figure, a multi-agent system gives you a mystery: did the researcher fetch the wrong document, did the analyst miscalculate the percentage, did the writer misquote the analyst, or did the editor change the number during polishing?

To answer that in two minutes instead of two hours, your tracing system must record a hierarchical span for every agent run, every handoff payload and every tool call under a single `trace_id`.

It is food traceability on a supermarket pack that tells you the exact farm, batch and packing line a box of strawberries came from.

Without end-to-end traces, teams waste days blaming the wrong prompt.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What do you need in place to quickly find which agent in a team introduced a wrong fact?

choices.text: A single log line that prints only the final answer shown to the user
Guessing which agent is usually worst and editing its prompt at random
Deleting all intermediate state as soon as each node finishes
End-to-end tracing that records every agent's inputs, tool calls and handoff payloads under one shared trace ID

questions.explanation: Hierarchical traces let you inspect the exact input and output of each agent in the chain to pinpoint where the fact went wrong.

bites.title: Evaluating the team and each agent separately
bites.body:
Testing a multi-agent system requires two levels of evaluation: **end-to-end team evals** and **component-level agent evals**.

End-to-end evals test whether the whole system turns a user request into a good final result. Component evals test each agent in isolation with fixed test inputs: given this exact research brief, does the researcher find the right three facts; given these exact facts, does the writer produce an accurate draft?

It is testing a racing car both by timing a full lap of the circuit and by testing the brakes and engine on a workshop rig on their own.

If an end-to-end test fails, component evals tell you which specialist broke.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why do you need both end-to-end team evaluations and isolated per-agent evaluations?

choices.text: Per-agent evals replace the need to ever test the whole workflow together
End-to-end evals cost zero tokens to run
You cannot pass test inputs to a single agent on its own
End-to-end evals measure overall user outcome, while per-agent evals isolate which specialist or handoff caused a regression

questions.explanation: Component evals let you test and tune each specialist quickly and deterministically, while end-to-end evals verify that the handoffs work together.

bites.title: A single agent is the baseline to beat
bites.body:
Before you build a five-agent crew, build the best single agent (or simple prompt chain) you can and measure it on your evaluation set.

Modern frontier models have large context windows, strong reasoning and reliable tool calling. A huge proportion of tasks that needed a complex multi-agent setup two years ago are now handled faster, cheaper and more accurately by one well-structured agent or two chained calls with code checks in between.

It is checking whether one skilled tradesperson can finish the job in an afternoon before hiring a general contractor and four subcontractors.

If a multi-agent team does not clearly beat your single-agent baseline on quality, speed or cost, keep the single agent.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What should always be your baseline before committing to a complex multi-agent architecture?

choices.text: A team of twenty agents with no tools
A human typing answers by hand with no AI
A single well-prompted agent or simple prompt chain measured on the same evaluation suite
Having no evaluation suite at all

questions.explanation: A single agent or simple chain is cheaper, faster and easier to debug, so a multi-agent design must earn its complexity on the evals.
